items.question_text: A car of mass 1200 kg has \(150\,\text{kJ}\) of energy in its kinetic energy store. Calculate its speed. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

wrong.misconception: This stops before the square root: \(v^{2} = 250\), so \(v = \sqrt{250} = 15.8\,\text{m/s}\).
This loses the 2 that comes from the half. \(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2E_k}{m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 150\,000}{1200}} = 15.8\,\text{m/s}\).
The half goes the other way when you rearrange: \(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2E_k}{m}}\), not \(\sqrt{\dfrac{E_k}{2m}}\). That gives \(15.8\,\text{m/s}\).
This uses the energy in kilojoules. Convert first: \(150\,\text{kJ} = 150\,000\,\text{J}\), so \(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 150\,000}{1200}} = 15.8\,\text{m/s}\).

items.stem: A go-kart and its driver are moving at \([[v]]\,\text{m/s}\). There is \([[E]]\,\text{J}\) of energy in their kinetic energy store. Calculate their total mass.

feedback.no-square: This divides by the speed, not the speed squared. Use \(m = \dfrac{2E_k}{v^{2}} = \dfrac{2 \times [[E]]}{[[v]]^{2}}\).
feedback.no-half: This loses the 2 that comes from the half in \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}\). Use \(m = \dfrac{2E_k}{v^{2}}\).
feedback.half-wrong-way: The half goes the other way when you rearrange: multiply the energy by 2, don't divide by it. \(m = \dfrac{2E_k}{v^{2}}\).

items.question_text: A school bus of mass 8000 kg is travelling at \(10\,\text{m/s}\). Calculate the energy in its kinetic energy store.

wrong.misconception: This leaves out the half. Kinetic energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 8000 \times 10^{2} = 400\,000\,\text{J}\).
Square the speed: \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 8000 \times 10^{2} = 400\,000\,\text{J}\).

items.explanation: \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 8000 \times 10^{2} = 400\,000\,\text{J}\). When the bus brakes to a stop, this movement energy is used up by the brakes.

items.question_text: A delivery drone has a mass of 1500 g. It flies horizontally at \(12\,\text{m/s}\). How much energy is in its kinetic energy store?

feedback.a: This multiplies by the speed instead of the speed squared. With the mass in kilograms: \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.5 \times 12^{2} = 108\,\text{J}\).
feedback.d: This uses the mass in grams. Convert first: 1500 g = 1.5 kg, so \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.5 \times 12^{2} = 108\,\text{J}\).

items.explanation: Convert the mass to kilograms: 1500 g = 1.5 kg. Then kinetic energy \(= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.5 \times 12^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.5 \times 144 = 108\,\text{J}\).

items.question_text: A ball of mass 2 kg moves at 3 m/s. Which of its quantities has the value 6 kg m/s?

feedback.b: Kinetic energy is measured in joules: here it is \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 3^{2} = 9\,\text{J}\).
feedback.c: Weight is a force, measured in newtons.
feedback.d: The speed squared is 9, in m²/s².

misconception_map.c: slip: confused mass times speed with weight
misconception_map.d: slip: squared the speed without a reason

items.explanation: Mass × velocity = 2 × 3 = 6 kg m/s: that is momentum.

items.question_text: Car P has twice the mass of car Q. Car Q is moving twice as fast as car P. Which car has more energy in its kinetic energy store?

options.a: Car P, because it has more mass
options.b: Car Q, because the energy depends on speed squared
options.c: Neither: they have the same, because the two effects cancel
options.d: You cannot tell without the actual masses and speeds

feedback.a: Mass matters, but speed matters more: kinetic energy depends on speed squared. Doubling the speed multiplies the energy by 4; doubling the mass only multiplies it by 2. So car Q has twice as much.
feedback.c: The effects would cancel only if kinetic energy depended on speed, not speed squared. Doubling the mass doubles the energy, but doubling the speed multiplies it by 4, so car Q has twice as much.
feedback.d: You can compare without numbers. Doubling the mass doubles the kinetic energy; doubling the speed multiplies it by 2² = 4. So car Q has twice as much as car P.

misconception_map.a: slip: judged the energy by the mass alone
misconception_map.d: slip: thinks a comparison needs actual values rather than the proportional relationship

items.explanation: Kinetic energy is proportional to mass and to speed squared. Car P: 2 × mass, so 2 times the energy. Car Q: 2 × speed, so 2² = 4 times the energy. Car Q has twice as much kinetic energy as car P.

feedback.no-square: [[wrong]] J multiplies by the speed instead of the speed squared. Square the speed first: \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times [[m]] \times [[v]]^{2}\).
feedback.square-mass: [[wrong]] J squares the mass instead of the speed. Only the speed is squared: \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times [[m]] \times [[v]]^{2}\).

items.question_text: A trolley is rolling along a level floor. Which change would double the energy in its kinetic energy store?

options.d: Doubling both its mass and its speed

feedback.a: Doubling the speed multiplies the kinetic energy by 4, because it depends on speed squared.
feedback.c: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so a small increase in speed cannot double it.
feedback.d: Doubling both multiplies the kinetic energy by 2 × 4 = 8.

misconception_map.c: slip: underestimates the effect of a speed increase
misconception_map.d: slip: thinks the two changes add rather than multiply

items.explanation: Kinetic energy is proportional to mass, so doubling the mass doubles it.

items.question_text: A motorbike and its rider have a total mass of 150 kg. They travel along a straight road at \(8\,\text{m/s}\). How much energy is in their kinetic energy store?

feedback.a: This multiplies by the speed instead of the speed squared. Square the speed first: \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 150 \times 8^{2} = 4800\,\text{J}\).
feedback.c: This leaves out the half: \(150 \times 8^{2} = 9600\). Kinetic energy is half of that, \(4800\,\text{J}\).
feedback.d: This squares the mass instead of the speed. Only the speed is squared: \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 150 \times 8^{2} = 4800\,\text{J}\).

items.question_text: A cricket ball leaves the bowler's hand at \(30\,\text{m/s}\) and travels 20 m to the batter. As it leaves the hand, there is \(72\,\text{J}\) in its kinetic energy store. Calculate the mass of the ball.

wrong.misconception: This divides by the speed, not the speed squared. Rearranging \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}\) gives \(m = \dfrac{2E_k}{v^{2}} = \dfrac{144}{900} = 0.16\,\text{kg}\).
This loses the 2 that comes from the half. \(m = \dfrac{2E_k}{v^{2}} = \dfrac{2 \times 72}{30^{2}} = 0.16\,\text{kg}\).
The half goes the other way when you rearrange: multiply the energy by 2, don't divide by it. \(m = \dfrac{2 \times 72}{30^{2}} = 0.16\,\text{kg}\).
This uses the distance (20 m) instead of the speed. Kinetic energy depends on speed: \(m = \dfrac{2 \times 72}{30^{2}} = 0.16\,\text{kg}\).

misconception_map.0.36: slip: used the distance travelled instead of the speed

items.explanation: Only the speed and the energy are needed; the distance is not. Rearrange \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}\) to \(m = \dfrac{2E_k}{v^{2}} = \dfrac{2 \times 72}{30^{2}} = \dfrac{144}{900} = 0.16\,\text{kg}\).
